title: Rx.NET 7.0 Reduces Deployment Size by Splitting Windows UI Support
gist: Rx.NET 7.0 splits WPF/WinForms/UWP/WinRT integration out of System.Reactive into separate NuGet packages, removing up to ~90 MB of unused framework payload from self-contained Windows deployments; the release is maintained by UK consultancy endjin, which says it has now completed the maintenance roadmap it published when it took stewardship in January 2023.

insights.claim: Referencing System.Reactive in a self-contained or Native AOT .NET app with a Windows-specific TFM could pull the complete WPF and Windows Forms frameworks into the deployment output even when neither UI framework was used.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Hidden transitive framework dependencies are a real cost driver for edge/container/desktop distribution — watch which libraries force UI framework payloads into trimmed builds.
insights.quote: Referencing System.Reactive could cause the complete WPF and Windows Forms frameworks to be included in deployment output, even when the application did not use either UI framework.

insights.claim: endjin quantified the unused-dependency bloat from System.Reactive at roughly 90 MB without trimming, around 47 MB with trimming, and about 11 MB for Native AOT builds.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Concrete size deltas of this magnitude matter for bandwidth-constrained deployment models and give a benchmark for judging similar library-bloat claims.

insights.claim: Rx.NET 7.0 relocates UI functionality into four new NuGet packages — System.Reactive.Windows.Forms, System.Reactive.Wpf, System.Reactive.WindowsRuntime and System.Reactive.Uwp — so that apps not using those integrations need no source changes while affected self-contained deployments shrink substantially.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Package-splitting is becoming the standard remediation for AOT/trimming-hostile libraries; expect more ecosystem churn of this kind.

insights.claim: Rx.NET 7.0 keeps the old UI APIs in its runtime assemblies but strips them from reference assemblies, so components precompiled against Rx.NET 6.1 keep running while newly compiled code cannot accidentally take a Windows UI dependency.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: A reusable pattern for library maintainers who need to break a dependency graph without breaking installed binaries — reduces the migration cost of similar splits.
insights.quote: The older UI APIs remain in the runtime assemblies shipped in the NuGet package, but are removed from its reference assemblies.
insights.locator: The maintainers have tried to preserve binary compatibility

insights.claim: An analyzer shipped with System.Reactive 7.0 detects source code affected by the package split and recommends which new package to add, lowering the upgrade cost.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Tooling-assisted migration is the differentiator between an adopted breaking change and an abandoned one.

insights.claim: Rx.NET 7.0 drops .NET 6 and .NET 7 while continuing to support .NET 8, 9, 10, .NET Framework 4.7.2, .NET Standard 2.0 and UWP, and required a major-version bump purely because corrected OfType nullability annotations changed a signature without changing runtime behaviour.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Semver-driven major bumps inflate perceived breakage; read release notes before budgeting migration effort.

insights.claim: Projects still using packages.config can bypass the split entirely because that format does not distinguish NuGet ref from lib assets, and the maintainers explicitly do not support the configuration and may delete the compatibility code later.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Legacy tooling formats quietly defeat security- and size-motivated packaging changes — an audit item for enterprises on old .NET project systems.

insights.claim: Since endjin, a UK company, took over maintenance of Rx.NET in January 2023, releases have concentrated on modernisation and technical debt rather than adding large operator sets, and version 7.0 contains essentially one major functional change.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Corporate stewardship of orphaned OSS tends to prioritise debt paydown over features — sets expectations for roadmap velocity of similarly adopted projects.

insights.claim: endjin says version 7.0 completes the main goals of the maintenance roadmap it published on assuming stewardship, with future work possibly shifting to lower-allocation implementations, code generation, ref-like element support and additional operators.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: A stewardship roadmap finishing is an inflection point — either the project pivots to performance work or maintenance attention decays.

insights.claim: Rx.NET users had previously flagged missing Windows scheduler APIs in some target-framework combinations plus demands for better trimming, AOT support and clearer package documentation, and public discussion following the 7.0 release remains limited.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Community reception is not yet measurable; treat adoption claims about this release as unproven for now.
insights.quote: Public discussion specifically following the 7.0 release remains limited, so it is too early to draw conclusions about broader community reception.
